> Bumping this with test data. You mentioned it needs a lot of testing, and I've had Grimmory running against my real library, so I went through both sides of the contract rather than just the Grimmory one.
> 
> I found something that won't work. Multi-file audiobooks don't match, and the push skips them without saying anything.
> 
> FindBookByPath compares full relative paths. For a folder-based audiobook Grimmory reports the folder rather than a file, and for that same audiobook Chaptarr reports one row per track, so the two sides hand you:
> 
> ```
> Grimmory   (fileSubPath / fileName):
>   matt dinniman/this inevitable ruin - jeff hays + travis baldree
> 
> Chaptarr   (Path minus the root folder):
>   matt dinniman/this inevitable ruin - jeff hays + travis baldree/this inevitable ruin (001).mp3
> ```
> 
> Those can't be equal. FindGrimmoryBook walks every track of the book, matches none, returns null, and PushBook logs "not found in Grimmory library ... skipping". No metadata and no cover go across.
> 
> What's actually in the two databases for the same 102-track book. Grimmory's book_file, one row for the whole folder:
> 
> ```
> book_id  is_folder_based  rows  file_name                                         file_sub_path
> 224      1                1     This Inevitable Ruin - Jeff Hays + Travis Baldree   Matt Dinniman
> ```
> 
> Chaptarr's BookFiles, one row per track:
> 
> ```
> Id    EditionId  path
> 1625  23640      /audiobooks/Matt Dinniman/This Inevitable Ruin - Jeff Hays + Travis Baldree/This Inevitable Ruin (001).mp3
> 1626  23640      /audiobooks/Matt Dinniman/This Inevitable Ruin - Jeff Hays + Travis Baldree/This Inevitable Ruin (002).mp3
> ```
> 
> On my library that's 45 audiobook editions, 24 single-file and 21 multi-file (2 up to 102 tracks), against the matching 24 non-folder and 21 folder-based entries in Grimmory. The 21 multi-file ones fail, about half my audiobooks. Every ebook matches, because ebooks are one file per edition on both sides.
> 
> I haven't run the connector, so read this as the two databases rather than watching the push fail. But the comparison can't succeed as written.
> 
> The fix is small, and Grimmory already gives you the flag for it. Its BookFile DTO carries a folderBased boolean and GrimmoryBookFile doesn't deserialize it. Reading it lets you switch strategy for those rows and leave everything else alone.
> 
> ```diff
>      public class GrimmoryBookFile
>      {
>          [JsonProperty("fileName")]
>          public string FileName { get; set; }
>  
>          [JsonProperty("fileSubPath")]
>          public string FileSubPath { get; set; }
>  
> +        // Grimmory sets this for multi-file audiobooks, where FileName is the folder itself.
> +        [JsonProperty("folderBased")]
> +        public bool FolderBased { get; set; }
> +
>          public string RelativePath()
>          {
>              return FileSubPath.IsNotNullOrWhiteSpace() ? $"{FileSubPath}/{FileName}" : FileName;
>          }
>      }
> ```
> 
> ```diff
>      public GrimmoryBook FindBookByPath(GrimmorySettings settings, long libraryId, string relativePath, bool bypassCache = false)
>      {
>          var normalized = NormalizeRelativePath(relativePath);
>  
>          if (normalized.IsNullOrWhiteSpace())
>          {
>              return null;
>          }
>  
>          return GetLibraryBooks(settings, libraryId, bypassCache)
> -            .FirstOrDefault(b => b.AllFiles().Any(f => NormalizeRelativePath(f?.RelativePath()) == normalized));
> +            .FirstOrDefault(b => b.AllFiles().Any(f => MatchesPath(f, normalized)));
>      }
>  
> +    private static bool MatchesPath(GrimmoryBookFile file, string normalizedPath)
> +    {
> +        var candidate = NormalizeRelativePath(file?.RelativePath());
> +
> +        if (candidate.IsNullOrWhiteSpace())
> +        {
> +            return false;
> +        }
> +
> +        if (file.FolderBased)
> +        {
> +            // Chaptarr reports one row per track; the folder is the track's parent directory.
> +            var separator = normalizedPath.LastIndexOf('/');
> +
> +            return separator > 0 && candidate == normalizedPath.Substring(0, separator);
> +        }
> +
> +        return candidate == normalizedPath;
> +    }
> ```
> 
> I compiled this matching logic standalone against net10.0 and ran the current and proposed comparison against real strings from both databases, with your NormalizeRelativePath, RelativePath and root-stripping used verbatim. The two folder tracks go miss to match, and the single-file m4b and ebook cases stay matching, so nothing else moves. I haven't built the patch into Chaptarr itself.
> 
> GrimmoryLibraryChangeForwarder has the same problem in the other direction, in ResolveSidecarBookFile. It matches a sidecar named after the book against a Chaptarr file whose filename equals that name, and for a folder audiobook the tracks are named after the book plus a number, so the base names never match either. I don't know whether Grimmory writes that sidecar inside the folder book or beside it, so I'm not confident enough in the shape of the fix to hand you a diff for it. If it lands inside the folder, comparing the directory name is enough:

>              return _mediaFileService.GetFilesWithBasePath(directory)
> -                .FirstOrDefault(f => f?.Path.IsNotNullOrWhiteSpace() == true &&
> -                    Path.GetFileNameWithoutExtension(f.Path).Equals(baseName, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase));
> +                .FirstOrDefault(f => f?.Path.IsNotNullOrWhiteSpace() == true &&
> +                    (Path.GetFileNameWithoutExtension(f.Path).Equals(baseName, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) ||

items.title: Fix author-name collisions and series-set release searches
items.body:
#### Description

Fix two causes of empty book searches, reproduced on 0.9.958:

- When an author's catalogue contains a book named after the author, the sibling-title check mistakes the release's author credit for that book. For example, `Isaac Asimov The Naked Sun 2011 RETAiL EPUB eBook-NODE` is rejected as a different book when the catalogue also contains `Isaac Asimov`. Ignore a contradictory title that tokenizes to the author's name. Other sibling-title checks remain active, including `Foundation and Empire` versus `Foundation`.
- `Galactic Empire Series 3 Books Set` queries every packaging term and returns nothing, although the indexer has `Galactic Empire series by Isaac Asimov EPUB`. Remove trailing numeric box-set packaging from the query. For titles explicitly naming a series set, also allow a matching variant that retains `Series` and omits the retail book count. Reject that variant if the release adds a volume/count or another title, including under default Balanced matching. The selected catalogue title stays unchanged.

This does not disable quality, language, pack, existing-file or other identity checks. It does not add general multi-book import support.

#### Database Migration

No.

#### How was this tested?

- Added regression tests: three author-credit cases failed before the fix, and two shorter series-set cases failed before the set-matching change. All pass with the patch. Tests also cover different-book rejection, partial sets, individual volumes, ebook and audiobook release names, and unchanged ordinary search titles.
- Full `Chaptarr.Core.Test` suite on current `develop`: **3,040 passed** using .NET SDK 10.0.401 on macOS x64.
- Backported the same changes to the `v0.9.958` source for the live installation: **3,028 passed** in its full suite.
- Deployed the patched Core assembly in an image derived from the pinned 0.9.958 Docker image, with configuration and catalogue unchanged. Verified the running assembly hash and empty health-alert list.
- Repeated the live interactive searches through Chaptarr's API and UI. The Naked Sun changed from zero displayed releases to one approved EPUB. The Galactic Empire set changed from zero returned releases to one approved EPUB. Both report `downloadAllowed: true` and no rejections. No download/import was triggered for this validation.

Test command, after restore/build:

```sh
LANG=en_US.UTF-8 LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 dotnet test src/Chaptarr.Core.Test/Chaptarr.Core.Test.csproj -c Release --no-build --no-restore
```

Build/restore used `-p:WarningsNotAsErrors=NU1902` for the existing `Microsoft.Build.Tasks.Git` 8.0.0 advisory. The initial full run under the workstation's Portuguese locale hit an unrelated M4B duration-message assertion (`23,4m` versus `23.4m`); the English-locale run passed. Neither dependency versions nor that test were changed.

#### Screenshots (UI changes only)

No frontend changes.

items.title: Fix repeated grabs of failed Usenet releases
items.body:
#### Description

Reject a failed Usenet release when the same title is returned again for the same author, even if the indexer reports a different publication timestamp. This prevents automatic failed-download retries from repeatedly grabbing the same named release while preserving differently named replacement candidates.

Fixes #140

#### Database Migration

NO.

#### How was this tested?

items.title: Prefer English edition in ratings-based edition selection tiebreak
items.body:
## Bug

When an import list discovers a new author from one shelved book, Chaptarr pulls in that author's entire back-catalog as unmonitored stub `Book` rows. For each work, `EditionSelector` has to pick one edition to represent it in the local catalog — and that pick had no language preference at all: it ranked candidates purely by native-format match, then per-edition vote count.

`MetadataProfile.AllowedLanguages` only filters the candidate pool when it's explicitly configured. On the common unconfigured profile, every language passes through untouched, and a translated edition can end up with more votes on its own edition row than the original English one for the same work (e.g. all Spanish-reader votes on one edition row, while English votes are split across several English edition rows). The higher-voted foreign edition then wins and gets stored as the book's sole representative edition.

Concretely, this produced local catalog rows like:
- A book whose local title became `"<Title> [Spanish Edition]"`, its stored edition carrying Spanish narrator credits, despite an English edition of the same work being available
- A book whose local title became `"<Title> – <German subtitle>"`, similarly mismatched

Both cases trace to the same author-bibliography-refresh timestamp in the DB, confirming the bulk back-catalog path, not a one-off manual add.

This selector (`EditionSelector.SelectByNativeFormatThenRatings`, via `SelectMostRated`/`SelectRepresentativeFallback`) is shared by two call sites:
- `BookInfoProxy.SelectBestEditionAsMonitored` — the provisional pick made when converting an author's full back-catalog from provider data, explicitly commented as provisional ("Language ... filtering happen[s] later once the metadata profile is available")
- `AuthorLibraryService.SelectMonitoredEditionsForMediaType` — the later, profile-aware pick

Unmonitored bibliography stub books never get promoted to the second pass, so they stay stuck with whatever the language-blind provisional pick chose — permanently.

## Fix

Add a language-preference tiebreak ahead of vote count in `SelectMostRated` and `SelectRepresentativeFallback`: an edition with explicit English language wins, an edition with no language tag is treated neutrally (not punished for missing metadata), and any other explicit language loses. It's a soft default ordering key, not an exclusionary filter — a foreign-only candidate pool still falls back to picking by votes exactly as before, and a library where `AllowedLanguages` is explicitly restricted to something else still narrows correctly upstream in `EditionMetadataProfileFilter`.

Added tests in `EditionSelectorLanguageFilteringFixture` covering: English winning over a more-voted foreign edition for both audiobook and ebook media types, and the no-English-available fallback still picking by votes.

## Testing

Ran `dotnet test` (net10.0) locally: full suite passes, 3023/3023, 0 failures — including the 3 new tests in `EditionSelectorLanguageFilteringFixture`.

items.title: Disable Import Mixed Content checkbox once a root folder has assigned authors

#### Description

`RootFolderController.UpdateRootFolder` already fail-closes any root-folder type change (other than widening to `Mixed`) once an author's `AudiobookRootFolderPath` or `EbookRootFolderPath` matches the folder's path — intentional, given the history of author-path bugs in this area (#106, #112, #115, #88, #63, #28), and covered by the existing `RootFolderControllerTypeChangeFixture` tests, which I left untouched.

items.title: Fix OnUpgrade-only notifications never enabling and Discord empty username
items.body:
#### Description

- `NotificationDefinition.Enable` checked `(OnReleaseImport && OnUpgrade)` instead of `OnUpgrade` on its own, so a notification configured only for upgrades (e.g. "only tell me about upgrades") computed `Enable = false` and silently never fired, even though the API/UI showed the trigger checked.
- Discord's `CreatePayload` unconditionally set `Username = Settings.Username`, which is `""` when the field is left blank. Discord's webhook API rejects an empty `username` outright (`Must be between 1 and 80 in length`), and since `NullValueHandling.Ignore` only omits `null` (not `""`), the field was never actually dropped from the payload. The existing conditional re-assignment a few lines down (meant to guard exactly this) was already being overwritten by the unconditional initializer above it, so it was dead code.

Fixes #150

#### Database Migration
NO

#### How was this tested?
- Confirmed via API: a Discord notification created with only `onUpgrade: true` now returns `enable: true`.
- Confirmed via API: a Discord notification saved with `username` left blank now sends a test message successfully instead of Discord returning a 400 (`Username cannot be ""`).
- `dotnet build` succeeds with no new warnings/errors.

items.title: Back off retrying cover URLs that a CDN just rejected with 403
items.body:
#### Description

- `MediaCoverService` had no negative-caching/backoff for cover URLs a CDN has already rejected with `403 Forbidden`. Every rename, refresh, import, or RSS sync that touches a book/author re-attempts the exact same known-bad URL from scratch.
- On a library where multiple books share an overlapping/duplicate cover URL that Amazon/Goodreads' CDN is currently blocking, this becomes an unthrottled retry storm against that single host. `ManagedHttpDispatcher` caps outbound connections at `maxConnectionsPerServer: 12`, so the retry rate can exceed the pool and starve it.
- Observed impact: a `RenameAuthorCommand` covering ~1600 authors hung with zero progress for 15+ minutes (`message` field frozen on one author, no new log lines) while the app itself stayed fully responsive. Diagnosing via `/proc/<pid>/net/tcp` on the host showed several leaked `CLOSE_WAIT` sockets to another local service at the moment of the hang. Cancelling the stuck command via `DELETE /api/v1/command/{id}` cleared the `CLOSE_WAIT` sockets instantly and let every other queued command resume.
- Because each 403 is caught and logged rather than treated as fatal, the command never surfaces an error — it just silently stops making progress.

**Fix:** adds a 6-hour in-memory negative cache (`ConcurrentDictionary<string, DateTime>`) keyed by URL inside `GetImageResponse`, the single chokepoint both the author-cover (`DownloadCover`) and book-cover (`DownloadBookCover`) paths already funnel through. A URL that just 403'd is skipped with a synthetic `HttpException` (fast-fail, no network call) for the backoff window instead of being retried by every subsequent book/author referencing it — existing `catch (HttpException e) when (... Forbidden)` call sites are untouched and keep working exactly as before.

This doesn't fix the CDN-side blocking itself (out of Chaptarr's control), but it stops one blocked URL from being able to stall unrelated bulk operations across the whole library.

Fixes #152

#### Database Migration
NO

#### How was this tested?
- `dotnet build` succeeds with no new warnings/errors.
- Reproduced the original hang on a live instance (~1600 authors), confirmed root cause via `/proc/<pid>/net/tcp` (leaked `CLOSE_WAIT` to a same-host service) and log correlation (repeated `Book/Author cover download blocked (403 Forbidden)` for the same handful of URLs across different book IDs), and confirmed cancelling the stuck command immediately cleared the connection pool and resumed the queue — consistent with the fix's target.

items.title: Downloads fail to import when Chaptarr holds the same book twice
items.body:
#### Description

Chaptarr can end up holding the same book as two rows when two catalogue listings were never linked — for example one row built from a Hardcover work and one from a Goodreads work, with the same author, the same media type and the same editions underneath. The rows are harmless until something downloads. A completed download is grabbed for one row, the import matcher picks the other, and the tracked-download safety check rejects it with `Completed download was grabbed for 'X' … but import matched 'Y'`. The file sits in the queue as *import blocked* until someone hand-imports it. This makes the existing retarget-to-grabbed-book path recognise those rows, using the evidence a person uses: same edition title and a compatible narrator. One method restructured, one fallback added, six regression tests.

Addresses #111, where another user reported the same rejection independently. This fixes the import half of that issue — a tracked download lands on the row it was grabbed for — and leaves the row-creation half alone.

**A concrete example.** *Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets* (audiobook) in my library was rows `6698` (`hc:429306`, work title in German, the monitored one) and `6875` (`gr:6231171`). Every download for it failed the same way, three times over a month. When I counted, **20 books across all three authors** in the library had twin rows like this, so every grab for those books was a coin toss. This was blocking an automated grabber I run against Chaptarr.

**What already works, and what doesn't.** Chaptarr already has code for exactly this situation: `RetargetSameWorkMatchesToGrabbedBook` moves a decision from a same-work sibling row onto the row that was grabbed. It just can't see twin rows.

| Step | State |
|---|---|
| Tracked download's target book is known (`remoteBook.Books`) | ✅ |
| Import decision that landed on a different row is detected | ✅ |
| `CanRetargetSameWorkMatch` accepts rows that share a **work id** | ✅ |
| `FindEquivalentEditionForTargetBook` accepts editions that share an **ISBN / ASIN / edition id** | ✅ |
| Rows and editions that share neither, but are visibly the same book | ❌ — what this PR adds |

<details>
<summary>Technical detail</summary>

Both existing checks are identity-based:

```csharp
// CanRetargetSameWorkMatch
return WorkIdMatcher.WorkProviderIdMatches(targetBook, matchedBook);

// FindEquivalentEditionForTargetBook
return editions.FirstOrDefault(edition => BookEditionIdentity.EditionsMatch(edition, matchedEdition));
```

Twin rows exist precisely because their ids differ, and their editions come from different listings too. Measured on my library, for eight twin pairs: **0** shared ISBN/ASIN, **0** shared edition ids, but a same-title-and-narrator edition on both sides in 7 of 8.

The change:

- `CanRetargetSameWorkMatch` is split into `IsSameWorkRetargetCandidate` (different rows, same media type, same author) and the work-id check. The retarget loop now proceeds for any candidate and lets the edition lookup decide.
- `FindEquivalentEditionForTargetBook` tries the identity match first, unchanged, then `FindMetadataEquivalentEdition`: editions on the grabbed row whose normalised title equals the matched edition's, with a compatible `Format`. A known, different narrator never matches. An unknown narrator on either side is not evidence against the match. Exact narrator matches win over unknowns; within a group the monitored edition wins, then the lowest id.
- Titles and narrators are normalised with the existing `Parser.NormalizeTitle`, so `Philosopher’s` and `Philosopher's` compare equal and double spaces in narrator names don't matter.
- Generic titles (`untitled`, `unknown`) are excluded, because my library really does have two *Untitled* rows per format.
- When no equivalent edition is found, the explicit *"no equivalent edition exists … Refresh metadata and retry"* rejection is now raised only for rows that share a work id. Rows that share neither a work id nor an equivalent edition fall through to the plain tracked-download rejection as before.

</details>

**Deliberate choices worth flagging for review**

1. **Title + narrator is treated as sufficient evidence of the same work.** This is the judgement call most worth challenging. The bar I set is: same author, same media type, same normalised edition title, same format, and either the same narrator or no narrator known on one side. I could not construct a realistic pair of *different* books that passes all of that at once, and the "Untitled" guard covers the degenerate case I did find. If you'd rather require the narrator to be known on both sides, it's a one-line change and I'll make it.
2. **Rows that *do* share a work id are slightly looser now.** Before, a work-id sibling with no identity-matched edition was rejected with "no equivalent edition". Now a title-and-narrator edition satisfies it. I think that's what the rejection message was asking the user to achieve by hand; happy to gate the fallback to non-id siblings only if you disagree.
3. **The fallback lives in this service, not in `WorkIdMatcher` or `BookEditionIdentity`.** Those helpers are used for grouping and search elsewhere, and I didn't want a looser notion of identity leaking into paths I haven't measured.

**Blast radius.** Everything is inside `RetargetSameWorkMatchesToGrabbedBook`, which runs only for tracked downloads (`downloadClientItem != null`) with exactly one expected book, and only on decisions that already matched a *different* row for the same author and media type. Manual imports, untracked folder scans, and cross-author or cross-format matches are untouched. Strict-edition validation (`EnforceTrackedDownloadExpectedEditions`) still runs after the retarget and can still reject it.

**Known gaps I deliberately did not fix**

- **Why the twin rows exist at all.** Refresh creates a new row for a provider work it can't link to an existing one, and this PR does nothing about that; it makes downloads land despite the twins. The root cause deserves its own change and I'd rather not fold it into an import fix.
- **Twins whose editions differ by a subtitle.** The fallback compares whole normalised edition titles, so `Fate Hollow Academy: Term 1` and `Fate Hollow Academy` (the pair in #111) would still be rejected unless the grabbed row also carries an edition with the shorter title. I did not loosen this to main-title matching, because `X: Term 1` and `X: Term 2` share a main title and are different books.
- **Only the tracked-download path.** A file imported by folder scan with no grab history has no "expected book", so nothing here applies.

While working on this I hit an unrelated restore failure on a clean checkout: `NU1902: Microsoft.Build.Tasks.Git 8.0.0 has a known moderate severity vulnerability`, promoted to an error by `TreatWarningsAsErrors`. It comes in through `Microsoft.SourceLink.GitHub` 8.0.0. I worked around it locally with `-p:NuGetAuditMode=direct` and left the package alone here, but CI may hit the same thing until SourceLink is bumped. Flagging it so it isn't mistaken for something this PR broke.

#### Database Migration

**NO.** No schema change of any kind. This reads `Edition.Title`, `Edition.Narrator`, `Edition.Format` and `Edition.Monitored`, all existing columns. No migration file, no change to `VersionInfo`.

#### How was this tested?

Native `dotnet` on Linux (.NET SDK 10.0.112), SQLite backend.

**Tests first, watched failing before the code existed.** Six tests in `DownloadedBooksImportServiceFixture`, driving the real `DownloadedBooksImportService.ProcessPath` end to end with the fixture's existing stubs, modelled on the actual rows from my library:

| Test | Asserts |
|---|---|
| `should_retarget_twin_row_match_by_edition_title_and_narrator_when_no_ids_are_shared` | the Chamber of Secrets case: import lands on the grabbed row and its edition |
| `should_not_retarget_twin_row_match_when_the_narrators_are_different` | Stephen Fry vs Jim Dale stays rejected |
| `should_not_retarget_twin_row_match_when_the_edition_titles_are_different` | a different book by the same author stays rejected |
| `should_treat_typographic_and_plain_apostrophes_as_the_same_edition_title` | `Philosopher’s` / `Philosopher's` match |
| `should_prefer_the_monitored_edition_when_the_matched_narrator_is_unknown` | unknown narrator picks the monitored edition |
| `should_not_treat_two_untitled_editions_as_the_same_work` | the generic-title guard |

The three "should not" tests passed before the fix as well; they pin behaviour I did not want to change.

**Counts, base `develop` (7a06004):** 3020 → 3026 (+6), 0 failing, Debug and Release.

**The tests catch the bug.** Reverting only the production hunk, tests untouched:

```
Failed should_prefer_the_monitored_edition_when_the_matched_narrator_is_unknown
Failed should_retarget_twin_row_match_by_edition_title_and_narrator_when_no_ids_are_shared

  Expected: True   But was: False        (decision.Approved)

Failed!  - Failed: 3, Passed: 3, Total: 6
```

**CI commands from `.github/workflows/build.yml`, run locally:**

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| Guard (repo) — no merge-conflict markers, `package.json` parses | pass |
| `version_guard.py sync` | pass — `0.9.964` |
| `version_guard.py monotonic --compare-ref origin/develop` | pass |
| `version_guard.py commit-hygiene --compare-ref origin/develop` | pass |
| `dotnet build src/Chaptarr.NoTests.sln --configuration Release` | **0 warnings, 0 errors** |
| `dotnet test … --configuration Release` | 3026 passed, 0 failed |
| `dotnet publish` (Console + Update) | pass |

Restore needed `-p:NuGetAuditMode=direct` for the reason above. No frontend files are touched, so the yarn steps aren't applicable.

**Against real data.** The edition-overlap figures and the "20 books with twin rows" count come from querying the `Books` and `Editions` tables of a live instance (736 books, three authors). The Chamber of Secrets rows in the tests carry their real ids, titles, provider ids and narrators.

**What I did not test.** I have not yet run a real tracked download through this build; that's the next thing I'll do on my own instance and I'll report back on this PR. I have not tested the PostgreSQL backend, though the change is pure in-memory. And I have not exercised a strict-edition book (`AnyEditionOk = false`) through the new path beyond the existing strict-edition tests still passing.

#### Screenshots (UI changes only)

items.title: Fix: Cached<T> leaks a Task.Delay timer per Set()/rolling-expiry touch on the same key
items.body:
#### Description

`Cached<T>.ScheduleTryRemove()` schedules a new `Task.Delay(lifeTime).ContinueWith(...)` on every `Set()` call (and every rolling-expiry `Find()`/`Get()`), but never cancels any delay already pending for that same key. On a long-lived cache that gets touched more often than its lifetime, orphaned delays are never cancelled and pile up indefinitely - each one harmless individually, but collectively a lot of live `Timer`/`Task` machinery sitting idle.

`MediaCoverProxy.RegisterUrl()` hits this directly: it calls `_cache.Set(hash, url, TimeSpan.FromHours(24))` unconditionally on every call, and it's called for every cover URL in every API response that includes book/author cover art (author lists, book lists, the queue view, etc).

**How this was found:** on a ~1,600-author / large-queue instance, the process was pegged at 200-300% CPU even at idle. `dotnet-counters` showed `dotnet.timer.count` steady around **15,180+** (a healthy instance should have dozens, not thousands), alongside a matching `dotnet.gc.heap.total_allocated` rate of 75-250MB/s.

A `dotnet-dump` heap snapshot (`dumpheap -stat`) showed near-identical live counts across several types, all traceable to one code path:

```
15,207  System.Threading.TimerQueueTimer
15,179  System.Threading.Tasks.Task+DelayPromise
15,179  System.Threading.Tasks.ContinueWithTaskContinuation
15,180  System.Action<System.Threading.Tasks.Task>
15,181  System.Threading.Tasks.Task+ContingentProperties
15,176  NzbDrone.Common.Cache.Cached<System.String>+<>c__DisplayClass16_0
```

`<>c__DisplayClass16_0` is the compiler-generated closure for `ScheduleTryRemove`'s `Task.Delay(...).ContinueWith(delegate {...})` lambda - confirming these were all orphaned expiry delays for the same `Cached<string>` instance (`MediaCoverProxy`'s cover-url cache), none of them ever cancelled.

**Fix:** track one pending removal per key (`ConcurrentDictionary<string, CancellationTokenSource>`) and cancel/dispose the previous one before scheduling a new one, so re-touching a key doesn't add another timer on top of whatever's already pending. Behavior is otherwise unchanged - the lazy expiry check in `Find()`/`Get()` and the `ClearExpired()` sweep are untouched; this only stops the proactive scheduled-removal delays from accumulating.

Fixes #157

#### Database Migration
NO

#### How was this tested?
- `Chaptarr.Common` builds clean.
- Added `CachedFixture` covering: repeated `Set()` on the same key stays at exactly one pending expiry timer, and an item still expires correctly after being repeatedly refreshed.
- `dotnet test --filter FullyQualifiedName~CachedFixture` passes (2/2).
- Not yet verified against a live restart of the reporting instance (that instance was mid a long-running, non-restartable `RefreshMonitoredDownloads` scan at the time and I didn't want to interrupt it) - happy to report back once that's safe to do.

#### Screenshots (UI changes only)
N/A

items.title: Interactive search finds nothing for a book titled "…, Book 4"
items.body:
#### Description

Interactive search returns nothing for any book whose monitored edition has an Audible-style title — `Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, Book 4` — on every Newznab and Torznab indexer, which includes everything proxied through Prowlarr. Release names almost never carry the series position, so all three query tiers look for text that isn't there. Chaptarr already solves exactly this for MyAnonaMouse, with a last-resort tier that drops the book number; this gives the Newznab generator the same tier. One property, one block in the request generator, eight tests.

**A concrete example.** The same indexer, the same categories, one minute apart:

| Query | Results |
|---|---|
| `Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, Book 4` (what Chaptarr sends today) | **0** |
| `Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire` | **14** |

Four monitored audiobooks in my library have titles of this shape and none of them had ever returned a single release, in the UI or through the API.

**What already works, and what doesn't.**

| Generator | Precise tiers | Last-resort tier without the book number |
|---|---|---|
| MyAnonaMouse | ✅ | ✅ — `MAM_SEARCH_FALLBACK_TERM … (book-number fallback)`, interactive only |
| Newznab / Torznab | ✅ | ❌ — what this PR adds |

<details>
<summary>Technical detail</summary>

`BookSearchCriteria.BookQuery` is built from `GetMainSearchTitle`, which only splits on `:` and `(`. A trailing `, Book 4` survives, and `GetQueryTitle` turns it into `…+Fire+Book+4`. The Newznab generator then sends that in all three tiers (`t=book&author=&title=`, `t=search&q=title+author`, `t=search&q=title`). The request a test captures today:

```
…/api?t=search&cat=3030,7020&extended=1&…&q=Harry%20Potter%20and%20the%20Goblet%20of%20Fire%20Book%204
```

The change:

- `BookSearchCriteria.BookQueryWithoutBookNumber` returns the query without a trailing book number, or `null` when the title has none (or is nothing *but* a book number), so callers can skip the extra tier. The pattern is MyAnonaMouse's `\s*,?\s*book\s+\d+\s*$`, extended to accept a fractional position such as `Book 0.5`.
- `NewznabRequestGenerator.GetSearchRequests(BookSearchCriteria)` appends one tier when `InteractiveSearch` is set and that property is non-null: `t=book&title=…` if the indexer supports book search, and `t=search&q=…` if it supports plain search.

`HttpIndexerBase` walks the tiers in order and stops at the first that returns releases (`if (releases.Any()) break;`), so the precise queries still run first and the new tier only fires when they find nothing.

</details>

**Deliberate choices worth flagging for review**

1. **Interactive search only, mirroring MyAnonaMouse.** This is the choice most worth challenging. A broader query is safe when a person — or anything calling the interactive endpoint — picks from the results, and less obviously safe when Chaptarr grabs on its own, so I kept automatic and RSS-driven searches exactly as they are. The cost is that an automatic search for these books still finds nothing. If you'd rather have it everywhere, it is a one-line condition and I'll change it.
2. **A new tier rather than stripping the suffix from `BookQuery`.** I tried stripping it in `GetMainSearchTitle` first. It is simpler, but it removes the book number from *every* tier, and it broke `should_add_book_number_fallback_as_last_tier_for_interactive_search` because MyAnonaMouse builds its precise tiers from the same helper. Keeping the precise query first seemed clearly right once I saw that.
3. **MyAnonaMouse keeps its own copy of the regex.** I did not move it onto the new property, to keep this change to one generator. Happy to fold the two together if you'd like a single source.

**Blast radius.** One new read-only property on `BookSearchCriteria`, and one added tier in one generator method. No existing tier, query or category changes. Indexers using other generators (MyAnonaMouse, FileList, Gazelle) are untouched. For a title without a trailing book number the chain is byte-for-byte what it was.

**Known gaps I deliberately did not fix**

- **Other suffix shapes.** `, Volume 2`, `, Part 2` and spelled-out numbers (`Book Two`) are not handled. `Part` in particular is often a real part of a title (*Henry IV, Part 2*), and I had no evidence for the others in my data.
- **The matcher is unchanged.** Releases found by the new tier are still judged against the monitored edition title, so some may be shown as soft-rejected. That is existing behaviour and felt like a separate conversation.

Unrelated to this change: a clean checkout currently fails `dotnet restore` with `NU1902` for `Microsoft.Build.Tasks.Git` 8.0.0 (via `Microsoft.SourceLink.GitHub` 8.0.0) because `TreatWarningsAsErrors` promotes the audit warning. I used `-p:NuGetAuditMode=direct` locally and left the package alone; I mentioned the same thing in #155.

#### Database Migration

**NO.** No schema change. The new property is computed from fields that already exist.

#### How was this tested?

Native `dotnet` on Linux (.NET SDK 10.0.112), SQLite backend.

**Tests first, watched failing before the code existed.** New fixture `NewznabRequestGeneratorFixture` (there was none), driving the real `NewznabRequestGenerator` with a stub capabilities provider and asserting on the URLs it produces:

| Test | Asserts |
|---|---|
| `should_add_a_book_number_fallback_as_the_last_tier_for_interactive_search` | one extra tier, containing the title and no `Book 4` |
| `should_search_the_fallback_by_title_and_by_query_when_the_indexer_supports_book_search` | both `t=book&title=` and `t=search&q=` |
| `should_search_the_fallback_by_query_only_when_the_indexer_has_no_book_search` | only `t=search` |

items.title: Allow conversion to be applied to books already in the library
items.body: #### Description MP3 → M4B conversion only ran for files arriving from a tracked download client, so a collection that predates Chaptarr could never be normalised to one format. `ImportApprovedBooks.ConvertBookGroupIfNeeded` returned early whenever there was no `DownloadClientItem`, and nothing else could reach the converter. This implements both suggestions from #109: 1. **The download id is now synthesised when no download client owns the import.** It was only ever a correlation key for progress tracking and the `.chaptarr-conversions` work folder, so it is derived from the book and edition instead (`chaptarr-local-{bookId}-{editionId}`). Keeping it stable means a retried conversion still finds the artifact retained by the previous attempt. On its own this makes manual import convert — see *Behaviour changes*. 2. **A `ConvertBookFiles` command (plus a bulk `ConvertAuthor`), scoped like `RenameFiles`.** `BookFileConversionService` takes existing `BookFile` rows, rebuilds import decisions with the book and edition already known, and hands them back to the import pipeline flagged as a library conversion. That reuses ffmpeg detection, the workspace free-space check, the concurrency semaphore, tagging, chapter insertion, destination naming and the recycle bin rather than duplicating any of it. Also added: - `GET /api/v1/convert?authorId=&bookId=` — previews what would convert, and why a file would be skipped (no conversion target on the profile, target not allowed by the profile, already M4B, missing from disk, Calibre-managed). - A **Convert Files** toolbar action on the author and book detail pages, with a preview modal modelled on the existing Organize/Retag modals. Three design decisions worth reviewing: - **A library conversion replaces only the files it converted.** Reusing the manual-import path was tempting, but `manualReplaceExisting` sweeps in *every other file on the book* — converting an audiobook would have deleted the book's eBook. Hence the new `LocalBook.IsLibraryConversion` flag, with replacement scoped to the conversion's own source paths. - **It bypasses quality gating.** The profile that wants everything as M4B is usually the same profile that disallows MP3, so gating would reject the library's own files before they reached the converter. This matches how manual imports and forced grabs are already treated. - **Selection is per book, not per file.** Every convertible file of a book becomes one output file, so converting 5 of 18 tracks would leave the book half MP3 and half M4B. The modal selects whole books, and the service expands a partial `files` selection to the whole edition (pulling in only siblings that would convert anyway). Detached conversion jobs remain limited to tracked downloads. They signal completion by pushing `ProcessMonitoredDownloadsCommand`, which has no way to resume a library conversion, so manual imports and library conversions convert inline on the calling thread — the path manual imports would already have taken. #### Behaviour changes - **Manual imports now convert** when the quality profile has a conversion target. This follows directly from fix (1) and is what `ConvertToQualityId` reads like it promises, but it is a change for anyone currently relying on manual import bypassing conversion. Happy to gate it behind a separate opt-in if you would rather it stayed opt-in. - **`DownloadedBooksScan` of a folder with no tracked download now converts too**, for the same reason — it is the other caller that passes a null `DownloadClientItem`. This matches the profile setting's own help text ("After download, convert compatible files…"). Note that the `hasRejectedTrackedDownloadDecisions` guard only applies to tracked downloads, so an untracked folder with some unmatched files will convert the files that did match. - **Library rescans are not affected.** `DiskScanService` goes through `ImportOrchestrator` and never calls `ImportApprovedBooks.Import`, so a scheduled rescan will not start converting an existing library on its own. `ImportApprovedBooks.Import` has exactly three callers: `ManualImportService`, `DownloadedBooksImportService`, and the new `BookFileConversionService`. - `ConvertBookFiles` / `ConvertAuthor` declare `RequiresDiskAccess` and `IsLongRunning`, so a large conversion run serialises against other disk commands (rescan, rename, download import) the same way `RenameAuthor` does. That is deliberate — it is writing into the library — but it does mean a long run holds the disk lane. On the "adjacent" point in #109: `ConvertMp3ToM4b` is already mostly neutralised — migration 076 clears it and `QualityProfileResource` derives it from `ConvertToQualityId`. Only the DB column and two `en.json` strings linger. I left it alone rather than touch migrations in this PR. Fixes #109 #### Database Migration NO. No schema changes, no new migration. `ConversionJob` rows are unchanged — library conversions do not create them. #### How was this tested? Built and tested from source on Linux (.NET 10.0.401, Node 22): - `dotnet build src/NzbDrone.Core/Chaptarr.Core.csproj` — clean - `dotnet build src/Chaptarr.Api.V1/Chaptarr.Api.V1.csproj` — clean - `dotnet test src/Chaptarr.Core.Test/Chaptarr.Core.Test.csproj` — **3033 passed, 0 failed**, including the 13 new tests - `yarn build` — compiles clean - `yarn typecheck` — clean - `yarn check-translations` — all `translate()` keys present in `en.json` - `yarn lint` — no new errors introduced (verified per-file against the pre-change baseline; the new `frontend/src/Convert/` files are lint-clean) - `stylelint` — clean on the new `frontend/src/Convert/*.css` New test fixture `BookFileConversionServiceFixture` (13 tests) covers eligibility and the skip reasons, per-edition grouping, the `IsLibraryConversion` / `replaceExisting` contract, whole-book expansion from a partial selection, and not pulling in non-convertible siblings. **End to end, in Docker.** Built the image with the repo's own `Dockerfile.build` from this branch, exported without `.git` (the same as building from a GitHub tarball). The only changes were two local build workarounds, neither part of this PR: my sandbox's proxy CA certificate, and the `NuGetAudit` workaround described below. Ran it with a fresh config, and drove it through both the API and the real UI in headless Chromium. The image includes the real ffmpeg, m4b-tool and mp4v2 tools, so these are genuine conversions: | Scenario | Result | |---|---| | **Library conversion, API.** 3-file MP3 book already in the library; profile *Convert To* set afterwards; `ConvertBookFiles` sent with **only 1 of the 3 files** selected | One 60.0s M4B with 3 chapters at the file boundaries and correct title/artist/album tags. All 3 MP3s removed (whole-book expansion works) and their rows deleted. Originals landed in the Recycle Bin. No `.chaptarr-conversions` folder left behind. | | **Ebook safety.** The MP3s and an EPUB of the same book ended up on the **same edition** (manual import put them there) | **EPUB untouched**, on disk and in the DB. Under the old same-edition replacement rule this EPUB would have been deleted; this is the case the new `filesToReplace` narrowing exists for. | | **Upgrades disabled.** Default Audiobook profile has *Upgrade Allowed* off | Library conversion still proceeds, as intended for an explicit user action. | | **Manual import converts (fix 1).** Target set, then 2 MP3s manually imported | Imported directly as one 30.0s M4B with 2 chapters. Source MP3s are left in the incoming folder (non-destructive, same as the download path). | | **Book page UI.** Convert Files → modal → Convert | UI posts `{"name":"ConvertBookFiles","authorId":1,"bookId":3,"files":[…4 ids]}`; the book goes from 4 MP3 files to 1 M4B. | | **Author page UI.** Mix of convertible and already-converted books | Already-converted books show *Already M4B* with a disabled checkbox. Convert posts without a `bookId` and converts only the selected book. | | **Preview reasons.** No target set / target set / already M4B | *"Quality profile 'Audiobook' has no conversion target set"* → convertible → *"Already M4B"*. EPUBs are omitted from the list. | The UI run caught one bug of mine, a mis-styled select-all checkbox in the modal, fixed in the second commit. **Notes for reviewers:** - **`Dockerfile.build` fails on `develop` right now, independent of this PR.** `dotnet restore` stops with `NU1902: Warning As Error: Package 'Microsoft.Build.Tasks.Git' 8.0.0 has a known moderate severity vulnerability` (GHSA-23fw-v26w-5fgq). It comes in via `Microsoft.SourceLink.GitHub` 8.0.0 plus `TreatWarningsAsErrors`, and it fails the same way on the untouched `develop` commit. To build for testing I added `/p:NuGetAudit=false` to that one restore line locally; it is not part of this PR. Bumping SourceLink probably fixes it, and is worth its own PR. - Profile changes can take **up to 10 seconds** to show in the preview, because of `AuthorService`'s 10-second author cache. That is pre-existing and affects every profile-dependent feature. - Originals in the Recycle Bin keep the pre-existing upgrade-staging suffix (`….mp3.chaptarr-upgrade~`), so restoring one means renaming it. - If the converted M4B's folder name differs from the MP3s' folder, the old folder is left empty. Cosmetic; happy to add cleanup if you want it here. - Only tested with synthetic tone MP3s, not a real multi-hour audiobook. Conversion time and memory on long books are the existing converter's behaviour, which this PR does not change. #### Screenshots (UI changes only) **Convert Files** on the book page, next to Preview Rename and Preview Retag. Before: 4 MP3 files. The preview modal at author level: one convertible book, others already M4B with the reason shown. After converting: the book has a single M4B. --- **A note on AI:** taking you up on the disclosure paragraph in the template — this change was written with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) (Claude Agent SDK), using **Claude Opus 5** (`claude-opus-5`) at **`xhigh`** reasoning effort. The investigation, design decisions, implementation, tests and this description were all AI-generated; I reviewed them before opening the PR. Please scrutinise it as hard as you like — the three design decisions called out above and the manual-import behaviour change are the places I'd start. The end-to-end runs above used synthetic MP3s, so a real multi-hour audiobook is the remaining gap.

One downside of this that I see is that I believe this will reset all stats for these books in downstrem consumers/libraries like ABS, etc. So for instance, if you're half way through your audiobook and convert it to m4b from mp3 in chaptarr, your progress is gone. But, if you use ABS (not sure, I'll have to check, or you can and reply that's helpful!) if you convert that same book it keeps/stores your progress?

I will have to test that thoroughly, but my use of ABS is long as the directory doesn't change, causing it to re-index or create a new entry in ABS. I don't lose my progress.  But I've done this inside of ABS using its ability to merge M4B.

Thanks, good catch. I tested it against Audiobookshelf, and you were right for one specific case. That case is now fixed in the PR.

**Short version:** Audiobookshelf ties listening progress to the book's *folder* (its library item), not to the audio files inside it. Progress survives a conversion as long as the M4B stays in the folder the MP3s were in. It's lost when the M4B lands in a different folder, because ABS then sees a brand-new book, and the old one shows as missing.

The PR originally put the converted M4B where Chaptarr's naming scheme says the book should live. For a library that predates Chaptarr (the main audience for #109), that's often a different folder name from the existing one, so progress was lost in exactly the case that matters most. I've pushed a fix: **library conversions now happen in place**, the same way ABS's own M4B tool does it.

### Results

ABS 2.36.1, same library folder as Chaptarr. Each book had progress set at **1:15 of 2:00** before converting:

| Scenario | Where the M4B landed | ABS after conversion | Progress |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chaptarr, book already in a Chaptarr-named folder | same folder | same item, now 1 M4B | ✅ kept at 1:15 |
| Chaptarr **before the fix**, book in a pre-Chaptarr folder (`… (Unabridged) [MP3]`) | new Chaptarr-named folder | old item **missing**, new item created | ❌ new item has none |
| Chaptarr **after the fix**, same pre-Chaptarr layout | same folder | same item, now 1 M4B | ✅ kept at 1:15 |
| ABS's own M4B encoder (for comparison) | same folder | same item, now 1 M4B | ✅ kept at 1:15 |

So after the fix, converting in Chaptarr behaves the same as converting in ABS as far as progress goes.

### What changed

New commit: **Keep library conversions in the book's existing folder**

- A library conversion writes the M4B into the folder the source files are already in. Naming is applied to the file name only.
- Disc subfolders (`CD1`, `Disc 2`, …) resolve to their parent book folder, which is how ABS reads them as one book.
- Anything that doesn't form one book folder inside the root folder (files spread across sibling folders, outside the root, loose in the root) falls back to normal naming.
- Downloads and manual imports are unchanged. Organize/Rename still moves a book into the naming scheme when you ask it to.

### How it was tested

1. Built the Docker image from this branch using the repo's `Dockerfile.build`, so the conversions used the real ffmpeg, m4b-tool and mp4v2.
2. Ran Audiobookshelf 2.36.1 in a second container, pointed at the same library folder, with its folder watcher on (the default).
3. Put MP3 audiobooks (4 × 30-second files each) into Chaptarr's library, including one moved into a pre-Chaptarr-style folder name with Chaptarr's records pointing at it there.
4. Scanned them into ABS and set listening progress to 75 seconds (62.5%) on each through ABS's API.
5. Converted with Chaptarr's new `ConvertBookFiles` command (what the Convert Files button sends), and one book with ABS's own M4B encoder for comparison.
6. Checked ABS twice: after its folder watcher reacted, and again after a full library scan. Both gave the same results. For each book I recorded whether the original item ID survived, what files it held, and the progress stored against it.
7. Reran the pre-Chaptarr-folder case on a fresh book with the fix applied.
8. Checked the converted file's timing: 120.05s against 120.00s of MP3s, with chapters at the original file boundaries. A saved position lands within a fraction of a second of the same spot in the story. m4b-tool adds about 0.05s per file boundary, so a book with dozens of files could drift a few seconds by the end.
9. Added unit tests for the in-place rule and its fallbacks. The full suite passes: 3039 tests, 0 failures.

### Caveats

- I only tested Audiobookshelf. Plex, Booksonic, Jellyfin and the rest weren't tested. Anything that keys books by folder should behave the same way, but I haven't confirmed that.
- Running Organize/Rename *afterwards* to move a book into the naming scheme will still look like a new book to ABS. That's true of any rename today and isn't specific to conversion.
- Where the originals go differs: Chaptarr sends the MP3s to its Recycle Bin (if one is configured), while ABS's encoder moves them into ABS's metadata folder.

(Tested with Claude Code, same as the rest of the PR.)

I found this while testing on my own Synology library. A long conversion only showed *"Converting 'Harvest' to M4B (1/1)"*, with no progress. Cancel in System → Tasks did nothing, because the conversion handler ignored the task's cancellation token.

items.title: Tell users how to fix authors skipped by bulk sync-monitoring
items.body:
#### Description

Fixes #161. The bulk Author Editor's "Sync Monitored Audio/eBooks" action silently skips any author missing one of the two root folder paths (`AudiobookRootFolderPath`/`EbookRootFolderPath`), reporting only an aggregate count with no indication of what to do next.

**Correction from the original version of this PR:** I initially assumed the frontend bulk editor had no way to set root folder paths at all, and considered adding a new UI control for it. That assumption was wrong - Author Editor already has a Root Folder bulk-set field (`AuthorEditorFooter.js`, backed by `RootFolderSelectInputConnector`), the same way it already supports bulk quality/metadata profile. It's just gated behind the page's media-type filter tab (Audiobooks / eBooks / All), same as quality and metadata profile are, so it only applies to one media type at a time - you can't set both root folders in a single action. That's the actual reason people hit the "both root folders required" skip: they set one via the bulk editor and assume that's enough, or don't realize the fix already exists in the UI.

So no frontend change is needed here - the fix is just telling people the real, already-supported steps instead of vague or (in the previous revision of this PR) actively wrong guidance:

> Sync was enabled for N author(s). M author(s) were skipped because both audiobook and ebook root folders are required. In Author Editor, switch the media type filter to Audiobooks, select the skipped authors, and set a Root Folder (this only assigns the path - it won't move any files unless you choose to). Repeat with the filter set to eBooks, then re-run Sync Monitored Audio/eBooks.

#### Database Migration
NO

#### How was this tested?
Updated the existing unit test in `AuthorEditorMissingRootHydrationFixture.cs` to assert on the new warning text. `dotnet test --filter FullyQualifiedName~AuthorEditorMissingRootHydrationFixture` - 5/5 passing.

Did not test the frontend live (no running instance in this sandbox) - no frontend files were touched, so this is a backend-only string change plus a matching test update.

items.title: perf(refresh): stop refetching Book+Author+Editions+Files per book during author refresh (#163)
items.body:
#### Description

`RefreshBookService.PublishEntityUpdatedEvent` called `_bookService.GetBook(id)` unconditionally for every book that changed during an author refresh - a full `Book + Author + Editions + BookFiles` reload, even though the author-level refresh already batch-loaded `Editions`/`BookFiles` for every book up front (`RefreshAuthorService.HydrateLocalChildrenForRefresh`), and `remoteData` (the author) is already in memory and identical for every book in a single author-scoped refresh call.

On a large library this produced a very large number of avoidable per-book queries. Measured via `pg_stat_statements` on a live instance (204s window, mid-refresh): 254,056 calls to `Authors JOIN Books WHERE Books.Id = $1` and 233,131 calls to `Editions WHERE BookId = $1`. This is a direct contributor to why authors with very large catalogues (e.g. Charles Dickens, 10k+ books) can take hours to refresh, and starve other commands of chaptarr's single disk-access slot for the duration.

Reuse the already-hydrated entity when its `Editions`/`BookFiles` are already loaded and its `Author` is already set, instead of re-querying. Falls back to the original full `GetBook()` fetch when something is genuinely missing (a merge target fetched via `GetEntityByForeignId`, or a direct single-book refresh call that didn't pre-hydrate), so behavior for every other caller/subscriber is unchanged.

Also fixes a related footgun found while testing this: `Book.Author` / `.Editions` / `.BookFiles` are backed by `LazyLoaded<TParent,TChild>` proxies that transparently issue a DB query the *first time* the materializing property is read. A naive `== null` check on those properties fires the exact query it's trying to detect. The fix checks the non-materializing `Lazy*.IsLoaded` flag instead, and pre-assigns `book.Author` before any code path can read it for the first time.

Fixes # (part of #163, tracked under #173)

#### Database Migration
NO

#### How was this tested?
- Built and ran in an isolated container against a full template copy of a production `chaptarr-main` database (real library, largest author has 10k+ books), so as not to touch any live data.
- Confirmed a `RefreshAuthor` run completes without errors/regressions.
- No behavior changes intended for any other `BookUpdatedEvent` subscriber: the published event still carries a fully-hydrated `Book` in every case, just sourced from memory instead of the database when possible.
- Subsequently deployed to the live instance this was profiled on, alongside the other PRs in this cluster (#167, #168, #172, #174) - a full `RefreshAuthor` pass over the whole library (400+ authors, including several with 3,000-10,000+ books) completed with no errors.

#### Screenshots (UI changes only)
N/A

items.title: perf(books): stop CloneStoredBook eagerly loading Author on every book save (#163)
items.body:
#### Description

`BookService.SaveEntity` runs unconditionally for every book processed during a refresh (not gated by whether the book actually changed), and its `UpdateMany` builds a "stored" comparison snapshot for each book via `CloneStoredBook`, which copied `Author = book.Author`.

`Book.Author` is a lazy-loaded property (`LazyLoaded<Book, Author>`, registered in `TableMapping` as a join back through `Books` by `Id`) - reading it on a freshly-queried row transparently fires:

```sql
SELECT "Authors".* FROM "Authors" JOIN "Books" ON ("Authors"."Id" = "Books"."AuthorId") WHERE ("Books"."Id" = $1)
```

Since this runs on every single book save, it fired once per book on every author refresh - regardless of whether the monitoring-sync logic that actually consumes the stored snapshot (`GetSyncUpdatesForMutations`) even needed it (that logic is gated behind `author.SyncMonitoredAcrossFormats` and typically applies to few authors).

The only place that later actually reads `Author` off a cloned/stored book (`PublishBookEditedEvents`) re-fetches it explicitly and cheaply via `GetAuthor(authorId)` - a simple primary-key lookup - before use, so the eager copy was pure overhead. Dropped it, keeping `AuthorId` (already copied), which is all of `CloneStoredBook`'s callers actually compare on.

A second commit in this PR fixes the same mechanism for the ASIN fields: `CloneStoredBook` also computed `ASIN`/`AudibleASIN` via `BookEditionIdentity.GetAsin()`/`GetAudibleAsin()`, which prefer an edition-level value over the book-level field by reading `book.Editions` - another lazy-loaded property, firing `SELECT Editions WHERE BookId = $1` on the same freshly-queried row, once per book, on every save. Neither field on the cloned snapshot is ever read anywhere (`HasMonitoringChanged` only compares the monitored flags), so both were dropped entirely.

Fixes # (part of #163, tracked under #173)

#### Database Migration
NO

#### How was this tested?
Measured on an isolated copy of a production database (unrelated to any live data, no live downloads/queue), same 2-minute `RefreshAuthor` window, processing the same 2 authors, comparing before this PR's changes vs. after (on top of #166):

|                     | before | after |
|---------------------|--------|-------|
| total DB queries    | 261,406 | 28,751 |
| DB execution time   | 4,868s  | 1,613s |
| Editions query      | 74,680  | 2,902  |
| Authors-join query  | 16,985  | 945    |

~89% fewer total queries and ~96% fewer of the specific Editions query, for the same amount of work done.

Subsequently deployed to the live instance this was profiled on, alongside the other PRs in this cluster (#166, #168, #172, #174) - a full `RefreshAuthor` pass over the whole library (400+ authors, including several with 3,000-10,000+ books) completed with no errors.

#### Screenshots (UI changes only)
N/A

Neither field on the cloned snapshot is ever actually read, so removed both.

Re-measured on the same isolated database copy, same 2-minute RefreshAuthor window, processing the same 2 authors (Jeffery Deaver, Homer):

items.title: perf(books): stop re-fetching RootFolders per work group during monitoring sync (#163)
items.body:
#### Description

`GetSyncUpdatesForMutations` (invoked via `SaveEntity` on every book save) calls `ApplyMutationSyncForWorkGroup` once per author-owned work group when that author has `SyncMonitoredAcrossFormats` enabled. That path could reach `EnsureOneMonitoredOnFormat` -> `CanEnableMonitoringForMediaType` -> `HasCompatibleRootFolderForMediaType`, which called `_rootFolderService.All()` fresh every time - an uncached full read of a small, rarely-changing table, repeated once per media type, per work group, per changed book.

Fetch `RootFolders` once per author (only for authors that actually have sync-across-formats enabled) and thread it through as an optional parameter. Every other existing call site (`ApplyInsertSyncDefaults`, `BuildReconcileSyncUpdates`, the direct `CanEnableMonitoringForMediaType` caller) is unchanged - the new parameter defaults to `null` and falls back to the original per-call fetch when not supplied, so behavior elsewhere is identical.

Fixes # (part of #163, tracked under #173)

#### Database Migration
NO

#### How was this tested?
Measured on an isolated copy of a production database (unrelated to any live data), on top of #166 and #167: the `RootFolders` query, which was running at roughly 2,000/min during a `RefreshAuthor` pass, dropped out of the top statements entirely after this change.

Subsequently deployed to the live instance this was profiled on, alongside the other PRs in this cluster (#166, #167, #172, #174) - a full `RefreshAuthor` pass over the whole library (400+ authors, including several with 3,000-10,000+ books) completed with no errors.

items.title: Speed up the slowest library queries on large databases
items.body:
#### Description

I profiled every SQL statement Chaptarr ran against my own library's database: 925 authors, 75k books, 130k editions, 12k book files, 650 MB. The profiling covered each main page of the UI plus startup. A handful of queries read far more of the database than their results need. This PR fixes the ones that an index or a join change can fix, and changes nothing else.

**Migration 108 adds four indexes and drops the two single-column indexes they make redundant:**

| Index | For | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `BookFiles (EditionId, Size)`, replaces `(EditionId)` | Author progress, the book index summary, every EditionId lookup | The file size and count roll-ups only read these two columns. BookFiles rows are wide (about 7 KB on average here, mostly `MatchProvenance` and `AllTags` JSON), so without this index each roll-up reads the whole table. |
| `Books (AuthorId, ReleaseDate, Id)` | The author index's next/last book | The `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY AuthorId ORDER BY ReleaseDate …)` queries can rank from the index instead of fetching every book row. |
| `Books (MediaType, LOWER(COALESCE(CleanTitle, Title, '')), Id, CleanTitle, Title)` | The Books page (paged, title-sorted) and its A–Z jump bar | With the same expression indexed, a page of 200 is read in order instead of sorting every book of that media type first. `CleanTitle` and `Title` are included so the jump-bar counts can be read from the index alone. Without them, that query walks the index and fetches every row out of order, and it came out slower than the sort it replaced. |
| `Editions (Monitored, BookId)`, replaces `(Monitored)` | Wanted → Missing and Cutoff Unmet | Both start from the monitored editions and only need `BookId`, so they no longer read edition rows. `Chapters` alone is 129 MB of the 219 MB Editions table here. |

**`MediaFileRepository.GetFilesByAuthor` and `GetFilesByBook` now INNER JOIN editions and books.** They filter on a book column, so they return the same rows as before. The difference is in the plan. With the shared `LEFT JOIN` builder, SQLite has to keep `BookFiles` as the outer table, so every call read every file row: `SCAN BookFiles`. `GetFilesByBook` runs per matching release in the decision engine (already-imported, repack and proper checks), and during imports, renames and retags. `GetFilesByAuthor` backs the author page's size numbers and file list.

#### Database Migration

YES. Indexes only; no data changes.

- `BookFiles`: adds `IX_BookFiles_EditionId_Size` and drops `IX_BookFiles_EditionId`.
- `Books`: adds `IX_Books_AuthorId_ReleaseDate_Id` and `IX_Books_MediaType_TitleSort` (an expression index, created with `Execute.Sql` because FluentMigrator can't express it; the same SQL works on SQLite and PostgreSQL).
- `Editions`: adds `IX_Editions_Monitored_BookId` and drops `IX_Editions_Monitored`.

Every step checks whether the index exists first. On my database the migration took about 1.7 s, mostly reading BookFiles once to build its index. The file grew by 12 MB (623 → 636 MB, 2%).

#### How was this tested?

**Unit tests.** The new `QueryPerformanceIndexesFixture` has 8 tests. It runs the real migrations into a fresh SQLite database, then:

- checks each index's columns and that the two replaced indexes are gone;
- captures the SQL that `BookRepository`, `MediaFileRepository` and `AuthorStatisticsRepository` actually send, and asserts on SQLite's query plan for it. Title page: uses the index, with no temp B-tree. Jump bar: covering index. Next/last book: covering index. Files by author and by book: no `SCAN BookFiles`. Author progress roll-up: covering index. Wanted's edition lookup: covering index.
- checks that `GetFilesByAuthor` and `GetFilesByBook` still return only that author's or book's mapped files, with edition, book and author loaded in the same query.

7 of the 8 fail without this change. The behaviour test passes both ways, as it should. The full `Chaptarr.Core.Test` suite passes: 3028 passed, 0 failed.

**My real database.** I ran a copy of my production database with indexer, download-client and notification credentials removed. The SQL numbers below use the same SQLite build Chaptarr bundles (e_sqlite3 3.50.4), loaded into a small harness. They are the median of repeated runs on an otherwise idle machine, and two separate runs agreed within about 10%.

| Query (what triggers it) | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| Books page, first 200 by title | 81 ms | 1.8 ms |
| Books page, 200 at offset 4,000 (scrolling down) | 406 ms | 2.1 ms |
| Books page, A–Z jump bar counts | 296 ms | 190 ms |
| Author index, next book for every author | 57 ms | 4.3 ms |
| Author index, last book for every author | 142 ms | 85 ms |
| Author progress, one author with 5,304 books | 47 ms | 32 ms |
| Author progress, one author with 36 books | 37 ms | 21 ms |
| Wanted → Missing, page / count | 136 / 134 ms | 75 / 70 ms |
| Wanted → Cutoff Unmet, page / count | 148 / 154 ms | 93 / 89 ms |
| `GetFilesByAuthor` (author with 15 files) | 45 ms | 0.7 ms |
| `GetFilesByBook` (book with 1 file) | 31 ms | 0.08 ms |

**Whole API requests** on the same database: a Debug build, each request replayed 5 times after a warm-up, median shown.

| Endpoint | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| `GET /api/v1/author/{id}/size/{mediaType}` | 43–50 ms | 5–11 ms |
| `GET /api/v1/bookFile?authorId=` | 45–55 ms | 6–8 ms |
| `GET /api/v1/book/paged` (title, 200 rows) | 250–287 ms | 169–186 ms |
| `GET /api/v1/book/buckets` | 416 ms | 279 ms |
| `GET /api/v1/wanted/missing` | 331 ms | 203 ms |
| `GET /api/v1/wanted/cutoff` | 367 ms | 263 ms |

`/api/v1/author` (about 1.9 s here) and `/api/v1/book?authorId=` (4.3–6.4 s for authors with 2–5k books) did not change. Their time goes to lazy loading and mapping, not to any one slow query. I'll open that as a separate issue.

**What it costs to write.** A refresh-style update of all 5,304 books of one author went from 38 ms to 105 ms, because Books has two more indexes to maintain. Changing monitoring on 6,454 editions and updating BookFiles sizes both stayed the same.

**PostgreSQL.** A fresh install on PostgreSQL 16 migrates cleanly to 108. The four indexes exist, the two old ones are gone, and `EXPLAIN` of the paged title query shows an Index Scan on `IX_Books_MediaType_TitleSort` with no sort. I have not load-tested on Postgres.

**What I tried and left out:**

- **`ANALYZE` / `PRAGMA optimize`.** About 10% faster on the current schema. With these indexes, though, it made the book-index summary query 2× slower (118 → 217 ms), so I left statistics alone.
- **A bigger page cache (`cache_size` 16 MB).** Consistently 20–30% slower on these queries here, so it stays at the default.
- **`temp_store=MEMORY`.** No measurable change.
- **`mmap_size=256MB`.** 10–50% faster across the board. But an I/O error on a memory-mapped database crashes the process instead of raising an error, and people run Chaptarr on NAS boxes and network mounts, so I didn't include it. It might be worth a separate discussion.
- **Setting the connection PRAGMAs once instead of on every open.** They add up to about 1–2% of SQL time, so it isn't worth the change.

**Notes for reviewers:**

- With `IX_Editions_Monitored_BookId` present, SQLite may use it instead of `IX_Editions_BookId_Monitored_Id` (from 105) for author progress's monitored-edition lookup. Both seek on the same two columns and return rows in `Id` order, and author progress got faster. The existing plan test for 105 is unaffected, because its fixture only creates that index.
- The expression index only helps if the query spells the expression the same way. The migration has a comment saying so. The plan tests would catch it if the title sort in `BookRepository` changed.
- Migration number: this takes 108, the next free one on `develop` today.

---

**A note on AI:** this change was written with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) (Claude Agent SDK), using **Claude Opus 5** (`claude-opus-5`) at **`xhigh`** reasoning effort. The profiling, the choice of indexes, the implementation, the tests and this description were all AI-generated; I reviewed them before opening the PR. The profiling hook used to find the hot queries was a local-only patch and is not part of this PR.

items.title: fix(queue): respect torrent preservation when removing downloads
items.body:
#### Description

Queue removal currently deletes a torrent and its files directly, bypassing the existing download preservation policy. A completed download that fails import matching can therefore be deleted when removed and blocklisted through the queue, even when its indexer has **Keep seeding permanently** (`NeverMoveOnImport`) enabled. Automatic cleanup already checks this policy; the queue endpoints do not.

Use `IDownloadImportModeResolver` to enforce the same policy for individual and bulk queue removal. A protected deletion returns HTTP 400 with instructions to choose **Ignore Download** or use `removeFromClient=false`. Bulk requests check every tracked download before changing any pending releases or client items, preventing partial deletion when a protected item appears later in the selection.

Ignoring, blocklisting, and changing category without client deletion remain available. Unprotected downloads retain their existing behavior. The guard also honors the resolver's existing protection for unmanaged torrents on clients configured with `CopyUnmanagedDownloads`.

**Intentional behavior change:** explicit queue deletion no longer overrides these opt-in preservation settings. Users who intend to delete a protected torrent and its files can still do so directly in their download client. This does not change client-side ratio/time limits or enable preservation settings by default.

Related: #129 clarifies preservation setting labels/help text; this PR adds enforcement to queue removal and does not depend on that wording change.

#### Database Migration

NO.

#### How was this tested?

Native Linux, .NET 10, based directly on current upstream `develop` (`7a06004`).

```sh
dotnet test src/Chaptarr.Core.Test/Chaptarr.Core.Test.csproj -c Release -p:WarningsNotAsErrors=NU1902
```

Full suite: **3,027 passed, 0 failed**; the production-reader fixture is skipped by the test runner. `NU1902` is demoted for the existing `Microsoft.Build.Tasks.Git` 8.0.0 advisory; no dependencies are changed.

Seven new regression cases exercise:
- Protected single-item deletion with and without blocklisting.
- Bulk preflight before pending-release or unprotected-client mutations.
- Ignoring, blocklisting, and changing category while preserving the client item.
- Unprotected client deletion retaining its existing behavior.

Reproduction:
1. Enable **Keep seeding permanently** for a torrent indexer and grab a torrent through it.
2. From the queue, choose **Remove from Download Client**, optionally with blocklisting.
3. Before: the torrent and files are deleted. After: the request is rejected before mutation, with instructions for retaining the torrent.
4. Choose **Ignore Download** instead; Chaptarr can stop tracking it without deleting the client item.

The same guard was also deployed and checked in a live Chaptarr instance: the queue/system APIs remained healthy, preservation settings persisted across restart, and the health endpoint reported no issues. No homelab configuration or deployment artifacts are included here.

items.title: perf(books): replace BuildWorkGroups's O(N^2) pairwise matching with a token-bucketed union-find (#163, #173)
items.body:
#### Description

Found via `dotnet-trace` against a live instance: while refreshing a "publisher as author" entity (Charles River Editors, 7,105 books, many near-duplicate reprints), `BuildWorkGroups` (used by `ApplyInsertSyncDefaults`, the insert-time counterpart of the cross-format-monitoring-sync logic fixed in #172) pinned chaptarr at 100%+ CPU for many minutes on a single call.

Unlike the other fixes in this cluster (#166/#167/#168/#172), which were called redundantly - once per book saved - this call site only runs once per insert batch. The problem here is that the algorithm itself is O(N^2): `BuildWorkGroups` compares every remaining book against every other remaining book via `WorkIdMatcher.CrossFormatSafeMatches`. For an author with thousands of books, that's tens of millions of comparisons in one call.

`CrossFormatSafeMatches` can only return true when two books share an identity token (drawn from the categories in `BookIdentity.GetProviderIdentityTokens` - work-level or edition-level, depending on same/cross media type); it never matches on title or anything else. So two books that share no token can never match and don't need to be compared at all.

The new implementation buckets books by token (O(N)), then only runs the real, unmodified `CrossFormatSafeMatches` - not a reimplementation of its rules - within each bucket, unioning matches with a union-find. Realistic token buckets are small (a handful of format/duplicate siblings), so the expensive comparison only ever runs on small candidate sets instead of the whole catalogue.

The original O(N^2) algorithm is kept, `internal`-only, as `BuildWorkGroupsReference`, purely so tests can assert the two produce identical output.

Fixes # (part of #163, tracked under #173)

#### Database Migration
NO

#### How was this tested?
- New `BuildWorkGroupsFixture`: hand-written cases for every semantic path the algorithm has to get right (shared work ids, shared edition ids, the cross-media-type work-only restriction, a transitive chain across different shared tokens, untokened books, empty/null input). Each case asserts the fast and reference implementations produce *identical* groupings, not just a hardcoded expected count, so the test catches a regression in either one.
- Full `Chaptarr.Core.Test` suite (3,016 tests) passes.
- Additionally verified out-of-band (not part of the committed suite, since it depends on ~1.4MB of extracted production data) with a differential run of both implementations against every book from five real large-catalogue authors on a live instance (Charles Dickens, Mark Twain, Nora Roberts, Lewis Carroll, Charles River Editors - 22,447 books total): identical groupings in every case.
- Deployed to the live instance this was profiled on: a full `RefreshAuthor` pass over 418 authors (including two ~4,000-book "publisher as author" entities, Alexandre Dumas at 3,777 books and Random House at 4,108) completed in ~45 minutes with no errors, each of those large authors clearing in well under a minute alongside dozens of others in the same window.

#### Screenshots (UI changes only)
N/A
